                                      IMPOSSIBILITY OF ALMOST EXTENSION

                                                           ASSAF NAOR




         A BSTRACT. Let (X, k · kX ), (Y, k · kY ) be normed spaces with dim(X) = n. Bourgain’s almost extension theorem
         asserts that for any ε > 0, if N is an ε-net of the unit sphere of X and f : N → Y is 1-Lipschitz, then there exists
         an O(1)-Lipschitz F : X → Y such that kF (a) − f (a)kY . nε for all a ∈ N . We prove that this is optimal up
         to lower order factors, i.e., sometimes maxa∈N kF (a) − f (a)kY & n 1−o(1) ε for every O(1)-Lipschitz F : X → Y.
         This improves Bourgain’s lower bound of maxa∈N kF (a) − f (a)kY & n c ε for some 0 < c < 21 . If X = `n      , then
                                                                                                                   p2
         the approximation in the almost extension theorem can be improved to maxa∈N kF (a) − f (a)kY . nε. We
                                                                                p
         prove that this is sharp, i.e., sometimes maxa∈N kF (a) − f (a)kY & nε for every O(1)-Lipschitz F : `n     2 → Y.



                                                      1. I NTRODUCTION
   The following theorem was proved by Bourgain in [Bou87]; see [Beg99] for a simpler proof.

Theorem 1 (Bourgain’s almost extension theorem [Bou87]). There exists a universal constant C ⩾ 1 with
the following property. Fix n ∈ N, ε > 0 and L > C . Suppose that (X, k · kX ) is an n-dimensional normed
space and that N is an ε-net of the unit sphere of X. Let (Y, k · kY ) be a Banach space, and let f : N → Y be a
1-Lipschitz mapping. Then, there exists an L-Lipschitz mapping F : X → Y satisfying1
                                                                   n
                                         max kF (a) − f (a)kY . ε.                                           (1)
                                          a∈N                      L
   It follows from [Bou87] (specifically, see the reasoning immediately after the statement of Theorem 2
in [Bou87]) that in the setting of Theorem 1 we must sometimes have maxa∈N kF (a) − f (a)kY ⩾ n c ε for
every O(1)-Lipschitz function F : X → Y, where 0 < c < 21 is a universal constant; we will recall the ap-
proach of [Bou87] and explain its features and limitations in Section 2. Theorem 2 improves this lower
bound via a route that is entirely different from that of [Bou87]; it demonstrates that Theorem 1 is sharp
up to lower order factors, e.g. in the important regime L¡ = O(1)
                                                               p it shows   that the conclusion of Theorem 1
cannot be improved to maxa∈N kF (a) − f (a)kY . n exp −K log n ε for some universal constant K > 0.

Roadmap. Theorem 2 will be proved in Section 3 and Theorem 4 will be proved in Section 4. In Section 2
we will discuss in greater detail various aspects of the almost extension problem for Lipschitz functions,
including comparing it to the classical Lipschitz extension problem, proving preliminary facts, and pre-
senting intriguing open questions. Thus, Section 2 has an introductory component, so those who prefer
to first read the proofs of Theorem 2 and Theorem 4 could skip directly to Section 3 and Section 4, re-
spectively. The proof of Theorem 4 in Section 4 does use parts of Section 2, namely Remark 5 and Propo-
sition 6 therein, but these could be read independently. Also, Section 3.1 presents variants of Theorem 2
when the source space is `np for 1 < p < 2, but the range p > 2 is treated (less satisfactorily) in Section 2.1.

                                  2. E XTENSION VERSUS ALMOST EXTENSION
    By proving Theorem 1, Bourgain’s achievement was not limited to merely establishing its statement.
It contains the noteworthy conceptual realization that his formulation of the almost extension problem
overcomes a barrier that previously precluded certain applications. Theorem 1 shows that by relaxing
the traditional requirement that the restriction of F to N coincides with f to the weaker requirement
that the restriction of F to N is close to f , it is possible ensure that F is O(1)-Lipschitz; this can fail if one
insists that F extends f , namely, in that case the Lipschitz constant of F must sometimes tend to ∞ as

                                                         2
n → ∞. At the same time, some important applications necessitate that F is O(1)-Lipschitz, and they
persist if F is O(1)-Lipschitz yet only sufficiently close to f on N , as demonstrated decisively in [Bou87].
   The input of the classical Lipschitz extension problem is two metric spaces (M, d M ), (Z , d Z ), as well
as a subset Ω ⊆ M. The goal is to determine if there is K ∈ [1, ∞) such that for every Lipschitz function
f : Ω → Z there is a function F : M → Z that extends f , i.e., F (ω) = f (ω) for all ω ∈ Ω, and such that
kF kLip ⩽ K k f kLip . Here, and in what follows, k·kLip denotes the Lipschitz constant. Let e(M, Ω; Z ) denote
the infimum over those K for which the above extension phenomenon holds, with the convention that
e(M, Ω; Z ) = ∞ if there is no such K . Write e(M; Z ) = supΩ⊆M e(M, Ω; Z ). Also, denote by e(M, Ω) the
supremum of e(M, Ω; Y) as Y ranges over all Banach spaces, and define e(M) = supΩ⊆M e(M, Ω).
   Finding geometric conditions on the triple (M, Ω, Z ) which ensure that e(M, Ω; Z ) < ∞, and moreover
obtaining upper and lower bounds on e(M, Ω; Z ), are important questions with applications in several
areas. The techniques that were developed to extend Lipschitz functions exhibit a rich interplay between
this area and other mathematical disciplines; see the monograph [BB12] for an indication of (part of ) the
many results along these lines that have been obtained over the past century.
   While e(M; Ω) is defined in terms of extension of mappings that can take values in all possible Banach
spaces, it has an intrinsic geometric characterization [Koz05, BB07, Oht09, AP20]. We will next explain a
generalization of this fact that applies to (but is more general than) the almost extension setting of The-
orem 1; this will clarify the geometric task at hand, and will also be valuable for the proof of Theorem 4.
For the sake of brevity and in order to avoid the need to treat issues (measurability, working with the
Lipschitz free space over Ω; see [Wea18]) that are by now well understood but could obscure the main
geometric content, our presentation (in Proposition 6) will be confined to the case when Ω is finite; this
is all that we will use here (in our setting, Ω = N is a net in the unit sphere of a finite dimensional normed
space, hence it is finite), but if the need to treat infinite subsets will arise in future investigations, then
it will be mechanical (thanks to [Koz05, BB07, Oht09, AP20]) to adjust the characterization accordingly
(using the Lipschitz free space instead of the Wasserstein-1 space).
   Suppose that (M, d M ) is a metric space and that Ω is a finite subset of M. Let W1 (Ω) be the space of
all the signed measures µ on Ω with vanishing total mass, namely µ(Ω) = 0. Equivalently, W1 (Ω) is the
hyperplane in RΩ consisting of all those µ : Ω → R that satisfy ω∈Ω µ(ω) = 0. For each µ ∈ W1 (Ω) de-
                                                                       P

note µ+ = max{µ, 0} and µ− = max{−µ, 0}, so that µ+ , µ− are disjointly supported nonnegative measures
on Ω with µ+ (Ω) = µ− (Ω) and µ = µ+ − µ− . The set of all possible couplings of µ+ and µ− is denoted
Π(µ+ , µ− ); it consists of all those nonnegative measures π on Ω × Ω that satisfy ω0 ∈Ω π(ω, ω0 ) = µ+ (ω)
                                                                                          P

and ω0 ∈Ω π(ω0 , ω) = µ− (ω) for every ω ∈ Ω. The Wasserstein-1 norm (sometimes also called the trans-

Proposition 6. Suppose that (M, d M ) is a metric space and fix a finite subset Ω ⊆ M. Fix also L ⩾ 1 and a
function α : Ω → [0, ∞). Then, the following statements are equivalent.
    (1) For every Banach space (Y, k · kY ) and every 1-Lipschitz mapping f : Ω → Y there is an L-Lipschitz
        mapping F : M → Y that satisfies kF (ω) − f (ω)kY ⩽ α(ω) for every ω ∈ Ω.
    (2) For every probability measure ν supported on Ω and every x ∈ M there is µx = µx (ν) ∈ W1 (Ω) such
        that kµx −µ y kW1 (Ω) ⩽ Ld M (x, y) for every x, y ∈ M, and kµω −(δω −ν)kW1 (Ω) ⩽ α(ω) for every ω ∈ Ω.

   Observe that if part (2) of Proposition 6 holds for some probability measure ν on Ω, then it also holds
for any other probability measure ν0 on Ω, as seen by considering {µx (ν0 ) = µx (ν) + ν − ν0 }x∈M . If α ≡ 0,
then Proposition 6 is the characterization of classical Lipschitz extension in [Koz05, BB07, Oht09, AP20],
while the almost extension setting of Theorem 1 and Theorem 4 corresponds to the special case of Propo-
sition 6 when α is the constant function which equals a positive multiple of ε, and Ω is the ε-net N .

Remark 7. To elucidate the geometric meaning of part (2) of Proposition 6, consider its variant in which
{µx }x∈M are probability measures on Ω instead of elements of W1 (Ω), and the analogous requirement is

     ∀x, y ∈ M,      kµx − µ y kW1 (Ω) ⩽ Ld M (x, y)   and       ∀ω ∈ Ω,    kµω − δω kW1 (Ω) ⩽ α(ω).      (10)

The ensuing proof of Proposition 6 shows mutatis mutandis that this is equivalent to the same assertion
as part (1) of Proposition 6, with the additional requirement that F takes values in the convex hull of f (Ω).
One can interpret the family of probability measures {µx }x∈M as a “randomized rounding scheme” that
associates to each point in the ambient space M a random element of the subset Ω. The first condition
in (10) is a consistency requirement for this rounding scheme, ensuring that nearby points distribute
themselves over Ω in manners that are close to each other in the sense of transportation cost. The second
condition in (10) is that each point of Ω distributes itself over Ω in a manner that is close (in the sense
of transportation cost) to the delta mass at that point; the case α ≡ 0, which corresponds to Lipschitz
extension (with the target constrained to be the convex hall of Ω), is the more stringent requirement that
each element of ω is “rounded” to itself with probability 1. In actuality, part (2) of Proposition 6 associates
to each point in the ambient space M an element of W1 (Ω), i.e., the difference of two disjointly supported
positive measures on Ω of equal total mass; this makes more use of the vector space structure of Y,
rather than only considering its convex structure, but we still think of the measures {µx }x∈M in part (2)
of Proposition 6 as a form of “stochastic retraction” of M onto Ω. We warn, however, that while in full
generality the behaviors of the extension problem into Y and the extension problem into conv( f (Ω)) ⊆ Y
are demonstrably different [Nao21], at present the relation between the two questions is for the most
part shrouded in mystery; these issues are discussed in greater detail in the forthcoming work [Nao21].

   Both parts of Proposition 6 are beneficial viewpoints for either proving the existence of an (almost)
extension, or for proving impossibility results; the latter is the topic of the present work. Our proof of
Theorem 2 directly rules out the existence of an almost extension as in part (1) of Proposition 6, while
our proof of Theorem 4 rules out the existence of a stochastic retraction as in part (2) of Proposition 6.
   There is a universal constant c > 0 such that every finite dimensional normed space X satisfies
                                            dim(X)c . e(X) . dim(X).                                      (13)
The upper bound on e(X) in (13) is a classical theorem of [JLS86] and the lower bound on e(X) in (13)
is due to the forthcoming work [Nao21]. It is a major problem to evaluate the asymptotic behavior (as
n → ∞) of e(X) for specific n-dimensional normed spaces X, but this goal resisted efforts for a long time.
The only normed space for which this was accomplished (up to lower order factors) is `n∞ , namely
                                       p              q
                                         n . e(`n∞ ) . n log n.                                        (14)
The lower bound on e(`n∞ ) in (14) is a classical combination of [Sob41] and [Lin64], and the upper bound
on e(`n∞ ) in (14) is due to [Nao17a]. Remarkably, even the Euclidean case X = `n2 remains a tantalizing
mystery, with the currently best known bounds being
                                              p               p
                                               4
                                                 n . e(`n2 ) . n.                                     (15)
The upper bound on e(`n2 ) in (15) is due to [LN05] and the lower bound on e(`n2 ) in (15) is due to [MN13]
(building on ideas of [Kal04, Kal12]). Determining the asymptotic behavior of the maximum of e(X) over

                                                           5
all possible n-dimensional normed spaces X is also a major longstanding open question; at present, the
                                                                                                        p
best known bounds are that it is at most a constant multiple of n and at least a constant multiple of n.
    The above discussion demonstrates that even in the seemingly “nice” setting of finite dimensional
normed (even Euclidean) spaces2, one cannot hope to be able to extend any 1-Lipschitz mapping to
a mapping whose Lipschitz constant does not tend to ∞ with the dimension (moreover, the rate must
sometime be of power-type). In contrast, in Theorem 1 Bourgain specifies a firm upper bound L that the
Lipschitz constant of F must not exceed, and shows that this is achievable by no longer insisting that F
extends f . Having such control on the Lipschitz constant of F is important for certain applications, most
notably the alternative tradeoff of Theorem 1 is used crucially in the proof of Bourgain’s discretization
theorem [Bou87], which is a quantitative version of an important rigidity theorem of Ribe [Rib76].
    When one is given a discretely-defined 1-Lipschitz mapping f , it is often desirable to obtain a mapping
F that “mimics” f yet is defined on the entire ambient normed space, so as to be able to apply continuous
methods, e.g. using differentiation or harmonic analysis. Any such reasoning that needs dimension-
independent bounds on the derivatives of F requires good control on kF kLip . The proof of Ribe’s theorem
in [Bou87] would utterly fail if the norm of the derivative of F were unbounded as n → ∞, because Ribe’s
theorem is all about dimension-independent bounds (its conclusion concerns the finite representability
of an infinite dimensional Banach space). At the same time, by [Bou87] the desired statement (Ribe’s
theorem, and even a quantitative version thereof ) follows if F is sufficiently close to f on the net N
(per the conclusion of Theorem 1), provided that f is O(1)-bi-Lipschitz, and N is fine enough, i.e., ε is
sufficiently small (the requirement of [Bou87] is ε ⩽ exp(− exp(O(n))), which remains the best known
bound in full generality; finding the optimal asymptotic behavior here is a fascinating open question;
see [GNS12, Ost13, LN13, HLN16, HN19]). Other applications of Bourgain’s almost extension theorem
appear in [Bou87, GNS12, NR17, NS21], some of which build on its simplified proof in [Beg99] (but we
checked that they could be deduced also using the original proof in [Bou87]); not all of these applications
belong to the above framework, e.g. [NR17, Corollary 22] is a statement in approximation theory.
    Beyond his demonstration of the highly significant application to Ribe’s rigidity theorem, Bourgain
took note of the potential of the aforementioned “twist” in Theorem 1 on the classical Lipschitz extension
problem, wherein one can specify the desired bound on kF kLip , by stating on page 158 of [Bou87] that
the existence of such a mapping “may already have considerable implications.” He proceeded to further
illustrate this by deducing Theorem 9 below on almost ellipsoidal sections. It is beneficial to recall this
specific application here because of its direct relevance to the present work, namely this is how a power-
type impossibility result in the context of Theorem 1 is obtained in [Bou87].
    Prior to stating Theorem 9, we introduce the following (somewhat ad-hoc, but convenient) terminol-
ogy that facilitates discussion of the parameters that occur in Theorem 1.
Definition 8 (almost extension pair). Let (X, k · kX ) be a normed space. A pair (L, A) ∈ [1, ∞) × [1, ∞) is an
X-almost extension pair if for every ε > 0, every normed space (Y, k · kY ), every ε-net N of the unit sphere of
X, and every 1-Lipschitz mapping f : N → Y, there exists an L-Lipschitz mapping F : X → Y that satisfies
                                               sup kF (a) − f (a)kY ⩽ Aε.
                                               a∈N
                      0
   Let (M, d M ), (M , d M0 ) be metric spaces. Suppose that they are bi-Lipschitz equivalent to each other,
namely that there exist a bijection ψ : M → M0 , a distortion D ⩾ 1, and a scaling factor s > 0 such that
                0
sd M (x, y) ⩽ d M (x, y) ⩽ D sd M (x, y) for all x, y ∈ M. The infimum over those D ⩾ 1 for which this holds is
called the bi-Lipschitz distance between (M, d M ) and (M0 , d M0 ), and it is denoted (when the metrics are
clear from the context) by d Lip (M, M0 ). Set d Lip (M, M0 ) = ∞ if (M, d M ), (M0 , d M0 ) are not bi-Lipschitz
equivalent. The bi-Lipschitz distortion of M in M0 is defined by cM0 (M) = infΩ⊆M0 d Lip (M, Ω).
   2Lipschitz non-extension phenomena were derived in many other settings as well. For example, see [NR17] for the currently
best-known general bounds in terms of the cardinality of Ω as well as [MM16] for algorithmic ramifications of such bounds.
Lipschitz non-extension theorems in the context of geometric group theory can be found in [BF09, RW10, NP11, BLP16].


                                                             6
   If (X, k · kX ) and (Y, k · kY ) are two isomorphic normed spaces, then their Banach–Mazur distance, de-
noted d BM (X, Y), is the infimum over those D ⩾ 1 for which there exists a linear operator T : X → Y such
that kxkX ⩽ kT xkY ⩽ DkxkX for all x ∈ X . If dim(X) = dim(Y) = n < ∞, then by compactness d BM (X, Y) is
attained, and by a standard application of the Rademacher differentiation theorem (see e.g. [BL00]) we
have d BM (X, Y) = d Lip (X, Y). If 1 ⩽ α < ∞ and d BM (`n2 , X) ⩽ α, then X is said to be α-Hilbertian; geometri-
cally, this is equivalent to the assertion that there exists an ellipsoid E ⊆ X such that E ⊆ B X ⊆ αE.

Theorem 9 ([Bou87]). For any D, K ⩾ 1 there exists ε ³ 1/ max{D 2 , K } with the following property. Suppose
that n ∈ N and (D, K /D) is an `n2 -almost extension pair. Let N be an ε-net of S n−1 and let Y be a normed
space for which cY (N ) ⩽ D. Then, Y has a 2-Hilbertian subspace H ⊆ Y such that dim(H) & n/D 4 .

   Theorem 9 is stated as [Bou87, Theorem 2] only in the special case K ³ n, because this is the statement
of Theorem 1, which was the only almost extension theorem that was available at the time; by Theorem 3,
                                                  p
we now know that we can actually take K ³ n here.3 However, the above formulation is exactly what
the proof in [Bou87] gives. The choice to discuss 2-Hilbertian subspaces was made arbitrarily in [Bou87],
though for any α > 1 an α-Hilbertian version follows formally; see [FLM77].
   Apart from the intrinsic geometric value of Theorem 9 (see e.g. [LM93, GM01] for surveys of the central
theme in modern Banach space theory of finding almost ellipsoidal sections), it was used in [Bou87] (see
equation (5) there) as follows to deduce an impossibility result for almost extension. Fix n ∈ N and p > 2.
By considering (a suitable rescaling of) the classical Mazur map [Maz29, BL00] we see that there is a
mapping φ : S n−1 → S `np that satisfies the following bounds for any 0 < ε < 1 and any ε-net N of S n−1 .

                                                                                      2         2

                                     ka − bk`n2 ⩽ kφ(a) − φ(b)k`np . pka − bk`n ⩽ pε p

Hence, if we choose p = 2 + 1/ log(2/ε), then it follows that c`np (N ) = O(1). By taking D, K ⩾ 1 such that
(D, K /D) is an `n2 -almost extension pair and D is a large enough universal constant, Theorem 9 implies
that if ε ³ 1/ max{D 2 , K } ³ 1/K , then `np has a 2-Hilbertian subspace H with dim(H) & n. However, the
maximal dimension of almost ellipsoidal sections of the unit ball of `np was studied in [BDG+ 77], where
it was shown that the above conclusion entails that
                                                                        2
                                                         dim(H) . n p .                                                        (16)
So, (log n)/ log(2/ε) ³ (1 − 2/p) log n . 1, and therefore we have K & n c for some universal constant c > 0.
   Recalling that the premise of the above discussion was that (D, K /D) is an `n2 -almost extension pair,
this reasoning of [Bou87] shows that the factor n in the conclusion (1) of Theorem 1 cannot be improved
to o(n c ). By optimizing the above reasoning, one sees that it is possible to take c = 41 − o(1) as n → ∞.
However, we checked that if instead of using Theorem 9 as a “black box” one incorporates its proof and
the proof of (16) in [BDG+ 77] into this reasoning in an optimal way, then it is possible to obtain the
better value c = 12 − o(1) as n → ∞. We omit the details of this optimization because it does not yield the
nearly optimal bound of Theorem 2. It is important to note that this drawback is inherent to Bourgain’s
approach, since the source space is `n2 , so by Theorem 3 it cannot yield a value of c that is larger than 12 .

Remark 10. The above approach of [Bou87] to proving impossibility of almost extension (hence, in par-
ticular, also impossibility of actual extension) is an interesting idea that, to the best of our knowledge,

   3The especially significant case D . 1 of Theorem 9, together with Theorem 3, has the following geometric interpretation.
                   p
For some ε ³ 1/ n, if an ε-net of S n−1 embeds with distortion O(1) into a normed space Y, then the unit ball of Y has an almost
ellipsoidal section of dimension proportional to n; this was obtained in [Bou87] with the weaker bound ε ³ 1/n. It remains open
to determine the slowest possible rate at which ε may tend to 0 with n such that the above conclusion still holds. If one aims to
get an almost ellipsoidal section of full dimension n, rather than allowing its dimension to be a smaller proportion of n, then this
is still possible, but now the best known bound [Bou87] is much weaker, namely this holds for some ε ⩾ exp(− exp(O(n log n))).
See [Bou87, GNS12, Ost13, LN13, HLN16, HN19, OR20] for more on these intriguing and longstanding discretization issues.


                                                                 7
differs from all other non-extension results that appeared in the literature. As such, it warrants fur-
ther scrutiny as a potential route towards related open questions; we defer such investigations to fu-
ture work. The aforementioned barrier c ⩽ 12 that makes this approach unsuitable as a potential route
towards Theorem 2 stems from its strong dependence on Euclidean symmetries, both in terms of the
proof in [Bou87], as well as its appeal to [BDG+ 77, FLM77]. Even in the Euclidean setting, we do not see
how this approach could possibly yield the sharp result of Theorem 4, namely it seems that the loss of an
unbounded lower order factor is inherent to the route that is taken in [Bou87].
2.1. Bi-Lipschitz invariance and the sphere compactum. It is natural to try to prove an almost exten-
sion theorem for a Banach space X, i.e., to determine specific X-almost extension pairs (L, A), by proving
such a theorem for some Banach space X0 with a good bound on d BM (X, X0 ), and somehow transferring
that theorem back to X itself. In the same vein, it is natural to try to deduce an impossibility result for
almost extension from nets in S X , from such a result for X0 . The following lemma is a small step in that di-
rection that yields in some cases the best bounds that we can currently achieve. As we will see later, there
is potential for great improvement here that relates to natural open questions of independent interest.
Lemma 11. Fix L, A, D, K ⩾ 1. Suppose that (X, k · kX ), (Y, k · kY ) are normed spaces and (L, A) is a Y-almost
extension pair. Let V ⊆ Y be a subspace of Y for which d BM (X, V) < D and there is a K -Lipschitz mapping
ψ : S Y → V such that ψ(y) = y for any y ∈ S V = V ∩ S Y . Then, (90K D 2 L, 9K A) is an X-almost extension pair.

    We will next discuss issues that arise when trying to prove (27). These issues also highlight subtleties
of the almost extension problem that are not present in the Lipschitz extension problem (observe that
for the latter problem, the analogue of (27) is trivially valid).
    Lipschitz almost extension is a nonlinear phenomenon about the geometry of spheres. So, the ap-
pearance of d BM (X, Y) rather than d Lip (S X , S Y ) in (27) could seem unnatural. In other words, (27) includes
a linearization statement by incorporating the linear quantity d BM (X, Y) into a nonlinear setting. We for-
mulated (27) as we did because such rigidity phenomena do occur quite often, and all the results on
almost extension that are currently known do obey (27). Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, evalua-
tions of d Lip (S X , S Y ) are not available in the literature. In our opinion, this is both a major omission and
a great opportunity to study the geometry of the sphere compactum, namely the space of all the spheres
of n-dimensional normed spaces, equipped with the multiplicative semi-metric d Lip . In contrast, the
Banach–Mazur compactum, namely the space of all n-dimensional normed spaces, equipped with the
multiplicative semi-metric d BM , is a deeply studied geometric object with rich structure; see [TJ89]. The
following lemma establishes rudimentary relations between d BM (X, Y) and d Lip (S X , S Y ).

Lemma 15. Suppose that (X, k · kX ) and (Y, k · kY ) are normed spaces with dim(X) = dim(Y) < ∞. Then,

    It suffices to justify the first inequality in (29) when k · kX , k · kY are norms on Rn that are smooth on
Rn r {0}, where n = dim(X) = dim(Y). Fix D ⩾ 1 and σ > 0. Suppose that ϕ : S X → S Y is a bijection that
satisfies σkx − x 0 kX ⩽ kϕ(x) − ϕ(x 0 )kY ⩽ Dσkx − x 0 kX for all x, x 0 ∈ S X . Using Rademacher’s differentiation
theorem [Rad19], there is x ∈ S X at which ϕ is differentiable. Thus, if x ∗ ∈ S X∗ is the supporting functional
of x, i.e., x ∗ (x) = 1, then there is a linear operator S : Ker(x ∗ ) → Y that satisfies σkx 0 kX ⩽ kSx 0 kY ⩽ σDkx 0 kX
for x 0 ∈ Ker(x ∗ ). Fix y ∗ ∈ S Y∗ whose kernel is SKer(x ∗ ) ⊆ Y and y ∈ S Y with y ∗ (y) = 1. Fix also λ > 0 and
define T : X → Y by setting T x 0 = λS(x 0 − x ∗ (x 0 )x) + x ∗ (x 0 )y for x 0 ∈ X, which is well defined because
x 0 − x ∗ (x 0 )x ∈ Ker(x ∗ ). Then, T is invertible and for y 0 ∈ Y we have T −1 y 0 = λ−1 S −1 (y 0 − y ∗ (y 0 )y)+ y ∗ (y 0 )x.
It is mechanical to check (using kSkKer(x ∗ )→Y ⩽ σD, kS −1 kSKer(x ∗ )→X ⩽ σ−1 and kx ∗ kX∗ = ky ∗ kY∗ = 1) that
kT kX→Y ⩽ 2λσD +1 and kT −1 kY→X ⩽ 2λ−1 σp           −1

   Among the many basic open questions about the sphere compactum, we mention the following.
      • What is the analogue of John’s theorem [Joh48] for the sphere compactum? Namely, how large
        can d Lip (S n−1 , S X ) be for an n-dimensional normed space (X, k · kX )? By Lemma 15 (using John’s
                                                                                           p
        theorem), the answer is bounded between universal constant multiples of n and n.
      • What is the analogue of Gluskin’s theorem [Glu81] for the sphere compactum? Namely, how large
        can d Lip (S X , S Y ) be for n-dimensional normed spaces (X, k·kX ) and (Y, k·kY )? By Lemma 15 (using
        Gluskin’s theorem), the answer is bounded between universal constant multiples of n and n 2 .
        What is the asymptotic growth rate (as n → ∞) of the typical bi-Lipschitz distance between the
        spheres of two independently chosen Gluskin bodies?

                                                                   11
      • For p, q ∈ [1, ∞], what is a the asymptotic growth rate as n → ∞ of d Lip (S `np , S `nq )? See [GKM66] for
        the asymptotic evaluation of the Banach–Mazur distance between `np and `nq .
    Even if we have a good upper bound on d Lip (S X , S Y ) at our disposal, whether in terms of d BM (X, Y) or
otherwise, then it is not clear how to transfer almost extension theorems (or theorems about the impossi-
bility thereof) between X and Y (unlike classical Lipschitz extension, for which this would be immediate).
    One relatively minor issue is that a bi-Lipschitz mapping need not send an ε-net to an ε0 -net of its im-
age for any ε0 > 0. This could be overcome in multiple ways, one of which is working with the notion of
(ε, δ)-nets, in place of the more typical use of ε-nets. Recall the following terminology. Let (M, d M ) be a
metric space. For ε, δ > 0, a subset N ⊆ M is called an (ε, δ)-net of M if it is ε-dense and δ-separated; the
former means that infa∈N d M (x, a) ⩽ ε for every x ∈ M, and the latter means that d M (a, b) ⩾ δ for every
distinct a, b ∈ N . Thus, the usual notion of ε-net (which we have been using tacitly) is the same as an
(ε, ε)-net. Fix two metric spaces (M, d M ), (M0 , d M0 ) and ε, δ, α, β > 0. Suppose that f : M → M0 is a map-
ping that satisfies the bi-Lipschitz condition αd M (x, y) ⩽ d M0 (x, y) ⩽ βd M (x, y) for all x, y ∈ M. Then,
the image f (N ) of any (ε, δ)-net N of M is a (βε, αδ)-net of f (M). So, a bi-Lipschitz mapping sends an
(ε, δ)-net to an (ε0 , δ0 )-net of its image for suitable parameters ε0 , δ0 > 0 (that are simple to control). Tradi-
tionally, almost extension theorems were proven for functions that are defined on ε-nets, but obtaining
(either existence or impossibility) results for (ε, δ)-nets rather than for ε-nets requires only mechanical
adaptations of their proofs. We chose not to do so here in order to avoid the need to track two parameters
throughout, but this could be easily taken up later if needed, by inspecting existing proofs (both for the
positive extension results in the literature, and the impossibility results of the present work).
    The following is a much more serious issue, which we do not know how to overcome and it may end up
being an inherent obstacle to the type of transference principle for almost extension that we are hoping
for. Fix normed spaces (X, k · kX ), (X, k · kX0 ), (Y, k · kY ) with dim(X) = dim(X0 ) < ∞. Suppose that s > 0 and
D ⩾ 1, and φ : S X → S X0 is a bijection satisfying skx − ykX ⩽ kφ(x) − φ(y)kX0 ⩽ D skx − ykX for x, y ∈ S X . If
N ⊆ S X is a net of S X and f : N → Y is 1-Lipschitz, then g = s f ◦φ−1 : φ(N ) → Y is also 1-Lipschitz. Fix L ⩾ 1.
Suppose that G : S X0 → Y is L-Lipschitz and denote α = maxu∈φ(N) kG(u)−g (u)kY . So, F = s −1G ◦φ : S X → Y
is (DL)-Lipschitz and satisfies maxa∈N kF (a) − f (a)kY ⩽ s −1 α. Thus, combining an almost extension the-
orem for X0 with a “vanilla” transference of the approximating mapping G back to X using the given
bi-Lipschitz equivalence produces a mapping F that approximates f in a controlled manner, but whose
Lipschitz constant is at least the distortion D, i.e., it cannot be specified arbitrarily in advance per Bour-
gain’s formulation of the almost extension problem. This encapsulates an important (and crucial for
applications) aspect of the new challenge that the almost extension problem raises. Nevertheless, the
fact that (27) is consistent with the known results on almost extension could be viewed as an indication
that there might a route towards these questions that is more circuitous that the above naive reasoning.

Remark 16. Extension from nets is an especially important instance of the Lipschitz extension problem,
so it is worthwhile to introduce the following notation. Given a metric space (M, d M ), define enet (M) to
be the supremum of e(M, N ) over all N ⊆ M which is an ε-net of M for some ε > 0. Note that if X is a
normed space, then by rescaling we see that enet (X) is given by the case ε = 1 of this definition, namely
enet (X) is the supremum of e(X, N ) over all N ⊆ X which is a 1-net of X. It is simple to show that
                                         enet (S X ) . enet (B X ) . enet (X).
If dim(X) < ∞, then it would also be worthwhile to study the quantity e(X, N ) for any specific 1-net N of
X, because by [BK98, McM98] nets of X need not be bi-Lipschitz equivalent to each other. If dim(X) = ∞,

                                                          13
then by [LMP00] any two nets of X are bi-Lipschitz equivalent to each other, but when the dimension is
infinite extending Lipschitz functions from nets sometimes exhibits pathological behavior [Nao15].5
   Basic questions remain open in the above context. E.g., what is the asymptotic growth rate of enet (`n2 )?
What is the asymptotic growth rate of the supremum of enet (X) over all n-dimensional normed spaces X?
   One could also formulate the almost extension problem for an arbitrary metric space M by asking for
those A, L ⩾ 1 such that for any ε > 0, any ε-net N of M, any normed space (Y, k · kY ) and any 1-Lipschitz
mapping f : N → Y there is an L-Lipschitz mapping F : M → Y that satisfies kF (a)− f (a)kY ⩽ Aε for every
net point a ∈ N . Investigating this question in such generality is a wide-open research direction. We warn
that when M = S X for some normed space X, this does not coincide with Bourgain’s formulation, which
asks for F to be defined on all of X rather than just on S X . But, it is simple to check that these formulations
are essentially the same if one does not mind losing universal constant factors.

  Here we will prove Theorem 2. The proof is short and entirely different from the approach of [Bou87]
that we recalled in Section 2. We will also discuss generalizations, and variants for `np when 1 < p ⩽ 2.

Remark 17. The above proof of Theorem 2 does not use fine properties of the crinkled ark. It only needs
a mapping from `n1 to an L q (µ) space that is q1 -Hölder with constant C 1 on S `n1 , and which sends any
pair of points in S `n1 that are at distance at least C 2 to points in L q (µ) that are at distance at least C 3 ,
where C 1 ,C 2 ,C 3 > 0 are constants independent of n ∈ N and 1 < q < 2 whose only impact is on the
resulting lower order factor. Similar statements could therefore be derived for other mappings, such as
the Mazur map [Maz29]. However, it would be independently interesting to find the best behavior in the
approximation lower bound (48) when using the crinkled ark: Is the lower order factor that this induces
in (2) necessary for the specific example of (powers of ) the crinkled ark that we consider here?
Remark 18. In the proof of Theorem 2, the role of L q (µ) as the target space is only through the validity
of (47). For this, it suffices for the target to have Enflo type q (using terminology of [BMW86]), and by the
remarkable work [IvHV20] this is equivalent to the target having type q in the linear sense (recall (17)).
   A quite substantial amount of bi-Lipschitz invariants is available as an outgrowth of the Ribe program
(see [Nao12, Bal13], though by now these surveys are out of date and more such invariants are known).
Due to the inherent quantitative nature of these invariants, they could in principle be used to prove the
kind of non-extension results that are the topic of the present work. Indeed, the above reasoning shows
how nonlinear type is useful for this purpose (applications of nonlinear notions of type to impossibility
of Lipschitz extension were found in other contexts in [JLS86, page 137] and [NP11, Section 8]). In the
course of the research that led to the present work, we systematically examined the relevance of all of the
aforementioned bi-Lipschitz invariants (of which we are aware) for the purpose of proving impossibility
of either Lipschitz extension or almost extension. This study is too lengthy to include here. It suffices
to say that while some of these invariants turn out to be applicable in our context, we only succeeded
to use them to derive bounds that are inferior to those that we present here. For example, we could
use metric X p inequalities [NS16, Nao16] to prove a variant of (20) which is asymptotically weaker in
terms of lower-order factors (as n → ∞) via a route that is completely different from how (20) is proven
here. At the same time, the use of many of those invariants (such as metric cotype [MN08]) to prove
(almost) non-extendability eludes us, and it would be worthwhile to obtain a principled understanding
of the reason why this is so. In some cases, we do see conceptual reasons for such difficulties. As an
example, consider the metric variant of the expander Poincaré inequality [LLR95, Mat97, MN14], which
is commonly used to remove lower-order factors (as done specifically for Lipschitz extension in [NR17]),
so a priori one could hope to use it to sharpen Theorem 2. However, it is impossible to realize expanders
faithfully as subsets of a low-dimensional normed space; certainly not bi-Lipschitzly [Nao17b], but even
weaker low-dimensional representations of expanders are impossible [Nao18, Nao19]. This appears to
be an inherent obstacle to proving lower bounds on (almost) Lipschitz extension from subsets of a finite
dimensional normed space that grow like a power of its dimension rather than logarithmically.
3.1. Approximate smoothing of powers of the helix. We stated and proved Theorem 2 separately be-
cause this is how we show that the original (full-generality) formulation of Bourgain’s almost extension
theorem is optimal up to lower order factors, and also because the crinkled ark is a canonical object. But,

                                                         16
the reasoning of the proof of Theorem 2 can be readily adjusted to yield almost optimal (up to lower or-
der factors) variants when the source space is `np for the range 1 ⩽ p < 2; the only difference is replacing
the crinkled ark by a θ-helix. Our proof breaks down when p = 2. Of course, Theorem 4 treats the end-
point case p = 2 even more satisfactorily (sharp up to constant factors), but we will prove Theorem 4 (in
Section 4) via a completely different and more involved reasoning that relies on Euclidean symmetries.
  Our next goal is to briefly explain how to adapt the proof of Theorem 2 so as to obtain its generalization
that we already stated in (25). Specifically, we will show that if A, L ⩾ 1, n ∈ N and 1 ⩽ p < 2 are such that

                                                                           17
            4. A PPROXIMATE STOCHASTIC RETRACTION FROM THE E UCLIDEAN SPHERE ONTO ITS NET
   Our goal here is to prove Theorem 4 by reasoning via the dual characterization in part (2) of Proposi-
tion 6. Prior to doing so, we will make some preparatory comments that will be used in the proof.
   Denote the standard scalar product on Rn by 〈·, ·〉 : Rn × Rn → R, namely 〈x, y〉 = x 1 y 1 + . . . + x n y n for

Remark 19. As an alternative route to Theorem 4, we checked that by implementing a suitable adaptation
of the strategy of the proof of [MN13, Theorem 1.17] (which requires, in particular, a setting of parameters
that differs from what was needed in [MN13]), one can obtain a different derivation of the sharp lower
bound (4). Even though this approach results in a more complicated example, it has the advantage that
the target space Y has Banach–Mazur distance O(1) to some subspace of `1 , and therefore, in particular,
it has cotype 2. In contrast, using [NS07] one can show that the Banach–Mazur distance between W1 (N ),
which is the target space that wep  use in the above proof of Theorem 4, and any subspace of `1 is at least
a universal constant multiple of log n. It is unknown whether W1 (N ), or even W1 (`2 ), has finite cotype
(see [Nao18, Question 7]); this is related to the old question [Bou86] whether W1 (R2 ) has finite cotype.

ing valuable corrections and suggestions.
